# In Praise of Friction: Notes on Latency, Maintenance, and the Weight of the World

## I. The Dream of the Frictionless

If you pay close attention to the vocabulary of the early twenty-first century, you will notice an almost religious devotion to a single adjective: *frictionless*. Payments are frictionless. Onboarding is frictionless. Commutes, grocery deliveries, romantic introductions, and the retrieval of human knowledge are all promised to us on a surface polished so fine that intention slides directly into outcome without a catch, a snag, or a second thought. In the mythology of contemporary design, resistance is always an error. A pause is a leak in the funnel. A moment of effort is a design flaw waiting to be smoothed away by the next software update.

It is an odd ideal, given that friction is the only reason anything in the physical universe can move on purpose.

In introductory physics, students learn early on that a world without friction would not be a utopia of effortless gliding; it would be a trap of absurd paralysis. Without static friction between the rubber of your sole and the concrete beneath you, taking a step would simply shoot your foot backward while your center of gravity dropped straight down. You could not hold a coffee cup, turn a doorknob, knot a shoelace, or strike a match. Music from a violin depends on the horsehair bow catching and releasing the rosin-dusted string hundreds of times a second. Nails stay in timber solely because the fibers press back against the steel. Everything we build, carry, or keep in place relies on two surfaces refusing to let each other go without a negotiation.

Yet our cultural imagination remains dazzled by the grease rather than the grip. We want the meal without the chopping, the intimacy without the awkward third conversation, the mastery without the afternoons of producing embarrassing work. When a piece of technology works well today, we praise it by saying it "disappears." The highest compliment we can offer a tool is that we never had to notice it existed.

There is real mercy in some of this, of course. Nobody romanticizes the bureaucratic labyrinth of renewing a driver's license by mail in 1984, or the aching back of hauling water from a well before indoor plumbing. Convenience has freed billions of hours of human life from sheer drudgery, and pretending otherwise is a luxury usually reserved for people who have never had to wash winter laundry by hand. The trouble is not that we have reduced unnecessary hardship. The trouble is that we have begun to mistake *all* resistance for hardship, and in trying to erase every seam from our lives, we are quietly erasing our sense of where things come from, what they cost, and what it means to inhabit a body in time.

Whenever an experience becomes completely seamless, the seams do not actually vanish. They are simply pushed out of sight, relocated into a basement, a warehouse, a server farm, or an ocean trench, where someone else—or something else—absorbs the drag on our behalf.

---

## II. The Geography of Latency

We like to speak of the digital realm as if it were made of weather. We store our photographs in "the cloud," stream music "through the air," and send messages instantaneously across hemispheres. The metaphors are deliberately weightless, airy, almost angelic. They invite us to imagine information as pure spirit, detached from dirt and distance.

The reality is considerably wetter, heavier, and more fragile.

Roughly ninety-eight percent of all intercontinental internet traffic does not travel through satellites hovering in the dark above us. It travels through fiber-optic cables resting directly on the floor of the ocean. Somewhere between the moment you tap "send" on a message to a friend in Lisbon and the moment their phone vibrates on a café table, your words are translated into pulses of laser light and fired through strands of ultra-pure glass roughly the width of a human hair. Those strands are bundled inside layers of copper, steel wire, petroleum jelly, and polyethylene until the whole assembly looks, in the deep ocean, about as thick as a garden hose.

There are hundreds of these cables draped across abyssal plains, snaking over submerged mountain ridges and down into trenches deeper than Everest is tall. Near the coasts, where the water grows shallow and dangerous, the cables are heavily armored and buried beneath the seabed by robotic plows. Even so, they break constantly—more than a hundred times a year across the globe. Early on, marine engineers noticed bite marks from deep-sea sharks, possibly agitated by the faint electromagnetic fields humming along the power conductors. Mostly, though, the culprit is mundane human industry: a cargo ship dragging its anchor through a storm, or the heavy iron doors of a commercial fishing trawler scraping across the mud.

When a cable snaps three miles below the surface, the cloud does not repair itself. A specialized cable-laying ship—one of only a few dozen in the world—steams out to the coordinates. Crews lower a grapnel into the blackness, hook the severed ends, haul miles of sodden cable back onto the deck, and hand it to technicians who sit in clean rooms aboard a pitching vessel, splicing hair-thin filaments of glass together under a microscope before lowering the whole repaired loop back into the dark.

Even when nothing breaks, light itself obeys a speed limit. Through glass, a photon moves about a third slower than it does in a vacuum. That means a signal traveling from New York to London and back requires a minimum physical round trip of roughly sixty to seventy milliseconds, even under ideal conditions, before you account for the routers, switches, and servers chewing on the packets along the way. To a human being reading an email, seventy milliseconds is invisible. To high-frequency trading firms, it is an eternity worth hundreds of millions of dollars. Companies have dynamited straight trenches through the Allegheny Mountains just to shave three milliseconds off the fiber path between Chicago and New Jersey.

I find something strangely comforting in this. Knowing that an email has to cross a mountain range or dodge a trawler's net restores a kind of dignity to the act of communication. It reminds us that nothing really escapes geography. Even our most ethereal inventions are tethered to geology, diesel fuel, salt corrosion, and the steady hands of a splicer working under fluorescent lights in the middle of the North Atlantic. The seamless surface on our glass screens is held aloft by an enormous, groaning apparatus of material friction.

---

## III. The Quiet Empire of Maintenance

Our history books are crowded with founders, inventors, and revolutionaries. We build statues for the person who first drew the blueprint, signed the charter, or stood on the stage announcing a breakthrough. We rarely build statues for the person who showed up every Tuesday for thirty-four years to oil the bearings, patch the mortar, and make sure the roof did not cave in during a hard freeze.

Innovation is photogenic; maintenance is invisible until it fails.

Consider the Golden Gate Bridge. There is a persistent urban legend that a crew of painters starts at the Marin County end, paints the entire span in its famous International Orange, and by the time they reach San Francisco, the weather has worn away the beginning, so they turn around and start over. The truth is less poetic and far more telling. The bridge is not painted end-to-end in a neat loop. Instead, a permanent team of ironworkers and painters roams the structure continuously, hunting for pockets where the Pacific salt fog has blistered the primer and begun eating into the steel underneath. They sandblast the rust back to bare metal, apply zinc coatings, and layer fresh paint over the vulnerable patches—day after day, decade after decade. The bridge does not simply *exist* as a completed object from 1937. It is an ongoing verb. If the painters walked away tomorrow, the Pacific Ocean would reclaim the whole span in a few generations.

We tend to imagine civilization as a collection of nouns: roads, grids, hospitals, libraries, laws. In practice, civilization is a fragile truce negotiated daily against entropy. Water wants to enter every basement. Roots want to buckle every sidewalk. Dust wants to choke every cooling fan. Left alone for even a few winters, an unheated house begins to smell of damp plaster and mice; within thirty years, saplings are pushing through the floorboards.

Software, despite its reputation for permanence, decays just as stubbornly. Programmers call it "bit rot" or "software rot"—not because the ones and zeros literally rust, though storage media certainly do, but because the ecosystem around a program shifts until old code can no longer talk to the world around it. Meanwhile, deep inside the foundations of global banking, airline reservation systems, and government benefits offices, billions of lines of COBOL written in the 1960s and 1970s are still humming along, processing trillions of dollars in daily transactions. They are maintained by a shrinking guild of graying engineers—and a handful of younger apprentices willing to learn an unfashionable tongue—who understand that rewriting the whole machine from scratch carries a catastrophic risk of breaking something nobody quite remembers building.

Perhaps the most honest monument to maintenance ever conceived stands in Mie Prefecture, Japan. The Ise Grand Shrine, dedicated to the sun goddess Amaterasu, is one of the holiest sites in Shinto. Yet the buildings standing there today are never very old. Every twenty years, in a cycle known as *Shikinen Sengu* that has continued with few interruptions for over thirteen centuries, the entire shrine complex is dismantled and rebuilt from scratch on an identical adjacent plot of land, using traditional joinery without a single nail.

At first glance, tearing down a masterpiece every two decades seems like an extravagant act of impermanence. In reality, it is a brilliant solution to the problem of memory. If you merely try to preserve a wooden building forever, eventually the timber rots and the artisans who knew how to shape it are long dead, leaving future generations to guess at how it was done. By rebuilding the shrine every twenty years, each generation of master carpenters passes the exact feel of the cypress plane, the angle of the mortise, and the rhythm of the roof thatch directly to the next. The real monument is not the wood. The real monument is the unbroken chain of practiced hands.

Western culture struggles with this kind of wisdom because we are obsessed with permanent triumph—fixing a problem *once and for all*, achieving a final state where the work is done. Maintenance insults that fantasy. It says the dishes will always return to the sink, the garden will always grow weeds, the democracy will always need defending, and the friendships you cherish will quietly starve if you assume yesterday's affection is enough to feed tomorrow. To make peace with maintenance is to make peace with the fact that caring for the world is never finished.

---

## IV. The Rooms Where Time Pools

If friction is the spatial resistance of the world, waiting is its temporal cousin. And few things reveal our current intolerance for drag more clearly than what happens to our nervous systems when we are forced to wait for forty-five seconds without a distraction.

Stand in line at a coffee shop or pause at a red light, and watch the choreography unfold. Within three seconds of stillness, hands drift reflexively toward pockets. Screens illuminate faces. It is as if unstructured time has become mildly toxic, an exposed wire we cannot bear to touch with our bare awareness. We no longer wait; we anesthetize the gap between events.

Engineers and psychologists have spent decades studying the strange elasticity of waiting, and their findings are wonderfully revealing about how the human mind measures friction. One of the most famous case studies comes from the Houston airport years ago. Passengers were flooding management with complaints about how long it took to retrieve their luggage at baggage claim. Airport officials poured money into hiring extra baggage handlers, bringing the average wait down to roughly eight minutes—well within industry standards. Yet the complaints kept coming.

When analysts actually timed the passengers' journey, they discovered that it took only one minute to walk from the arrival gates to the carousel, followed by seven minutes of standing around staring at an empty rubber belt. So the airport tried something counterintuitive. Instead of speeding up the luggage, they moved the arrival gates farther from baggage claim. Now passengers spent six minutes walking and only two minutes waiting at the belt. The total time remained identical, yet the complaints dropped almost to zero.

Occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time. Uncertain waits feel vastly longer than known, finite waits. That is why the humble progress bar on a computer screen is actually a small theater of psychological manipulation. Computer scientists at Carnegie Mellon once tested different visual styles of loading bars that all took the exact same duration to complete. They found that a bar moving smoothly at a constant pace felt noticeably slower than one that started sluggishly and accelerated toward the end—and even more remarkably, adding backward-moving diagonal stripes along the bar tricked human perception into believing the task finished roughly eleven percent faster. We do not mind the wait nearly as much as we mind the suspicion that nobody is driving the train.

Still, there is something slightly tragic about how thoroughly we have exiled boredom from our lives. Before pocket screens, waiting rooms were strange, accidental sanctuaries. You sat in a dentist's office leafing through a four-month-old magazine about woodworking or regional golf courses, listening to the hum of an aquarium filter and watching dust turn slowly in a bar of afternoon sunlight. You stood on a train platform letting your gaze wander over the brickwork of the opposite warehouse, noticing for the first time a ghost sign for a nineteenth-century flour mill painted above the roofline.

In those unscheduled pockets of latency, the mind had nowhere urgent to go, so it began rummaging through its own attic. Unfinished thoughts collided. A phrase from a conversation three days earlier suddenly made sense. You remembered to call your aunt. Neuroscientists now associate these moments of unfocused drift with the brain's default mode network—the circuitry involved in autobiographical memory, moral imagination, and creative synthesis. When we fill every stray twelve-second gap with an algorithmic feed, we do not actually gain more life. We just pave over the small meadows where our own thoughts used to graze.

Waiting forces us to confront the humbling fact that the world does not run on our personal clock. Bread has to rise. Bones have to knit. Grief has to move through seasons at its own stubborn pace, utterly indifferent to productivity hacks. There are certain transformations that cannot be rushed without ruining them, just as you cannot bake a loaf of sourdough in four minutes by turning the oven up to two thousand degrees. You only burn the outside and leave the center raw.

---

## V. Against Smoothness

A few years ago, I watched a friend teach himself to hand-plane a board of white oak. For the first hour, it was mostly an exercise in frustration. The blade chattered, dug in too deep, and tore ragged chunks out of the surface. He adjusted the iron by fractions of a millimeter, sharpened the bevel on a waterstone until it could shave hair from his forearm, turned the board around so he was working *with* the grain rather than against it, and tried again.

Then the sound changed. Instead of a harsh scrape, there came a dry, papery whisper—*shhhhhh*—and a translucent ribbon of oak curled up through the throat of the plane, smelling sharply of tannins and vanilla. The board beneath was suddenly glossier than sandpaper could ever make it, because a sharp blade shears wood fibers cleanly rather than abrading them into microscopic fuzz.

What struck me watching him was that the entire satisfaction of the moment depended on the oak pushing back. The tree had grown in wind and sunlight for eighty years, laying down dense winter rings and porous spring rings, twisting around a knot where a branch had once reached out. You could not bully the wood into compliance. You had to read its history with your palms and ears, adjusting your posture and pressure to meet its nature. Had the material been uniform, featureless plastic, there would have been nothing to learn and no joy in getting it right.

This principle reaches far beyond carpentry. Almost every craft or pastime that humans return to with lifelong devotion involves deliberately preserving a calibrated measure of resistance. Think of games: a golf course is simply a walk spoiled by sand traps, ponds, and absurdly small holes. If the goal were merely to put a white ball inside a cup as efficiently as possible, you could walk up and drop it in with your hand. The obstacles are not inconveniences standing in the way of the game; the obstacles *are* the game.

Writing works the same way. Anyone who has tried to put a complicated, half-formed intuition into clear sentences knows the peculiar agony of staring at a paragraph that refuses to cohere. You delete a clause, try a different verb, realize the logic is crooked, and discover that the thought you were so proud of in your head was actually hollow once dragged into daylight. That struggle is not a bug in the process of communication. It is the crucible in which vague feelings become actual thought. When you offload all the friction of drafting, wrestling, and revising onto a machine that spits out plausible prose in two seconds, you may end up with a tidy document, yet you bypass the very transformation that writing exists to produce inside the writer. You get the souvenir without having taken the trip.

Even our small physical preferences quietly testify against total smoothness. Why do so many people who work on sleek, silent laptops still spend unreasonable sums on fountain pens with toothy nibs, cast-iron skillets that weigh nine pounds and require seasoning, vinyl records that must be flipped after twenty minutes, or mechanical keyboards that click with a deliberate snap? It is easy to dismiss these habits as hipster nostalgia or fetishized consumerism, and sometimes they are. But beneath the aesthetic fashion lies a genuine sensory hunger. Glass touchscreens flatten every human activity—ordering toothpaste, breaking up with a partner, reading Tolstoy, filing taxes—into the exact same weightless tap of an index finger against cool silicon. Our hands, evolved over millions of years to feel bark, stone, fur, wet clay, and woven hemp, are starving for texture.

Smoothness promises comfort, yet too much of it produces a strange, bloodless vertigo. A landscape with no traction offers nothing to push off from, and nothing to hold onto when the wind rises.

---

## VI. The Grip on the Floor

Nowhere is the seduction of the frictionless more dangerous than in how we treat one another.

Other people are, by definition, high-friction. They arrive late. They misunderstand your favorite joke. They leave wet towels on the bed, hold baffling political opinions, grieve differently than you expect, and need help moving a sofa up three narrow flights of stairs on a Saturday morning when you wanted to sleep in. Every real human relationship requires an endless series of awkward negotiations between two sovereign worlds that never quite line up cleanly at the edges.

It is not hard to see why a culture trained on one-click convenience grows increasingly tempted to treat human connection as a user-interface problem. We curate our social circles the way we tune a streaming playlist, silently unfollowing or ghosting at the first sign of discomfort. We look for companions—and increasingly, even artificial companions—who mirror our moods without ever making an inconvenient demand, challenging our blind spots, or presenting us with the stubborn, irreducible otherness of a separate soul.

Yet what we love most in another person is rarely their seamlessness. It is their grain. It is the exact, idiosyncratic way they resist our assumptions and enlarge our world by refusing to be an echo of our own voice. A friendship forged only out of effortless agreement has no tensile strength; the first genuine storm snaps it clean in two. The bonds that endure are almost always the ones that survived a misunderstanding, endured a long dull season of ordinary maintenance, and kept showing up when it would have been much easier to slide away.

A few months ago, during an unexpected snowstorm, the power went out across my neighborhood for nearly two days. For the first hour, everyone felt mildly outraged, tapping dead light switches by reflex and refreshing cellular bars that refused to budge. Then, slowly, the pace of the street changed. Without Wi-Fi or streaming television, neighbors drifted out onto the front stoops with snow shovels and thermoses of soup. A retired electrician down the block loaned out battery lanterns. Someone dug an ancient board game out of a hall closet, and four of us sat around a kitchen table by candlelight, wearing wool sweaters indoors, listening to the wind test the window frames and watching wax pool in brass saucers.

Nobody wanted the power to stay off forever. When the furnace finally roared back to life on the second evening and the refrigerator hummed awake, we cheered. Modern infrastructure is a miracle, and I have no wish to live without warm showers, antibiotics, or the transatlantic glass threads carrying messages from people I love.

Still, I have thought often about those quiet forty hours—about how vivid the room felt once the invisible cushion of convenience thinned out just enough for us to feel the weather again. The cold had weight. The tea tasted sharper. The conversation wandered for three hours without anyone checking a screen to settle a minor trivia dispute, leaving the small mystery hanging pleasantly in the air between us.

Perhaps the wisest posture toward the world is not to reject ease, nor to worship hardship for its own sake, but to choose our frictions deliberately. To notice where resistance is merely cruel waste, and where it is the very thing giving shape, flavor, and gravity to our days. To remember the diver splicing glass in the dark ocean, the painter scraping rust above the bay, the carpenter reading the curve of an oak board, and the simple physics of a shoe meeting the pavement.

We are not meant to hover an inch above our lives, gliding effortlessly from birth to death without leaving a scuff mark. We are meant to press down, feel the ground push back, and use that grip to walk somewhere worth going.

Neuroscientists now associate these moments of unfocused drift with the brain's default mode network—the circuitry involved in autobiographical memory, moral imagination, and creative synthesis. When we fill every stray twelve-second gap with an algorithmic feed, we do not actually gain more life. We just pave over the small meadows where our own thoughts used to graze.

Waiting forces us to confront the humbling fact that the world does not run on our personal clock. Bread has to rise. Bones have to knit. Grief has to move through seasons at its own stubborn pace, utterly indifferent to productivity hacks. There are certain transformations that cannot be rushed without ruining them, just as you cannot bake a loaf of sourdough in four minutes by turning the oven up to two thousand degrees. You only burn the outside and leave the center raw.

---

## V. Against Smoothness

A few years ago, I watched a friend teach himself to hand-plane a board of white oak. For the first hour, it was mostly an exercise in frustration. The blade chattered, dug in too deep, and tore ragged chunks out of the surface. He adjusted the iron by fractions of a millimeter, sharpened the bevel on a waterstone until it could shave hair from his forearm, turned the board around so he was working *with* the grain rather than against it, and tried again.

Then the sound changed. Instead of a harsh scrape, there came a dry, papery whisper—*shhhhhh*—and a translucent ribbon of oak curled up through the throat of the plane, smelling sharply of tannins and vanilla. The board beneath was suddenly glossier than sandpaper could ever make it, because a sharp blade shears wood fibers cleanly rather than abrading them into microscopic fuzz.

What struck me watching him was that the entire satisfaction of the moment depended on the oak pushing back. The tree had grown in wind and sunlight for eighty years, laying down dense winter rings and porous spring rings, twisting around a knot where a branch had once reached out. You could not bully the wood into compliance. You had to read its history with your palms and ears, adjusting your posture and pressure to meet its nature. Had the material been uniform, featureless plastic, there would have been nothing to learn and no joy in getting it right.

This principle reaches far beyond carpentry. Almost every craft or pastime that humans return to with lifelong devotion involves deliberately preserving a calibrated measure of resistance. Think of games: a golf course is simply a walk spoiled by sand traps, ponds, and absurdly small holes. If the goal were merely to put a white ball inside a cup as efficiently as possible, you could walk up and drop it in with your hand. The obstacles are not inconveniences standing in the way of the game; the obstacles *are* the game.

Writing works the same way. Anyone who has tried to put a complicated, half-formed intuition into clear sentences knows the peculiar agony of staring at a paragraph that refuses to cohere. You delete a clause, try a different verb, realize the logic is crooked, and discover that the thought you were so proud of in your head was actually hollow once dragged into daylight. That struggle is not a bug in the process of communication. It is the crucible in which vague feelings become actual thought. When you offload all the friction of drafting, wrestling, and revising onto a machine that spits out plausible prose in two seconds, you may end up with a tidy document, yet you bypass the very transformation that writing exists to produce inside the writer. You get the souvenir without having taken the trip.

Even our small physical preferences quietly testify against total smoothness. Why do so many people who work on sleek, silent laptops still spend unreasonable sums on fountain pens with toothy nibs, cast-iron skillets that weigh nine pounds and require seasoning, vinyl records that must be flipped after twenty minutes, or mechanical keyboards that click with a deliberate snap? It is easy to dismiss these habits as hipster nostalgia or fetishized consumerism, and sometimes they are. But beneath the aesthetic fashion lies a genuine sensory hunger. Glass touchscreens flatten every human activity—ordering toothpaste, breaking up with a partner, reading Tolstoy, filing taxes—into the exact same weightless tap of an index finger against cool silicon. Our hands, evolved over millions of years to feel bark, stone, fur, wet clay, and woven hemp, are starving for texture.

Smoothness promises comfort, yet too much of it produces a strange, bloodless vertigo. A landscape with no traction offers nothing to push off from, and nothing to hold onto when the wind rises.

---

## VI. The Grip on the Floor

Nowhere is the seduction of the frictionless more dangerous than in how we treat one another.

Other people are, by definition, high-friction. They arrive late. They misunderstand your favorite joke. They leave wet towels on the bed, hold baffling political opinions, grieve differently than you expect, and need help moving a sofa up three narrow flights of stairs on a Saturday morning when you wanted to sleep in. Every real human relationship requires an endless series of awkward negotiations between two sovereign worlds that never quite line up cleanly at the edges.

It is not hard to see why a culture trained on one-click convenience grows increasingly tempted to treat human connection as a user-interface problem. We curate our social circles the way we tune a streaming playlist, silently unfollowing or ghosting at the first sign of discomfort. We look for companions—and increasingly, even artificial companions—who mirror our moods without ever making an inconvenient demand, challenging our blind spots, or presenting us with the stubborn, irreducible otherness of a separate soul.

Yet what we love most in another person is rarely their seamlessness. It is their grain. It is the exact, idiosyncratic way they resist our assumptions and enlarge our world by refusing to be an echo of our own voice. A friendship forged only out of effortless agreement has no tensile strength; the first genuine storm snaps it clean in two. The bonds that endure are almost always the ones that survived a misunderstanding, endured a long dull season of ordinary maintenance, and kept showing up when it would have been much easier to slide away.

A few months ago, during an unexpected snowstorm, the power went out across my neighborhood for nearly two days. For the first hour, everyone felt mildly outraged, tapping dead light switches by reflex and refreshing cellular bars that refused to budge. Then, slowly, the pace of the street changed. Without Wi-Fi or streaming television, neighbors drifted out onto the front stoops with snow shovels and thermoses of soup. A retired electrician down the block loaned out battery lanterns. Someone dug an ancient board game out of a hall closet, and four of us sat around a kitchen table by candlelight, wearing wool sweaters indoors, listening to the wind test the window frames and watching wax pool in brass saucers.

Nobody wanted the power to stay off forever. When the furnace finally roared back to life on the second evening and the refrigerator hummed awake, we cheered. Modern infrastructure is a miracle, and I have no wish to live without warm showers, antibiotics, or the transatlantic glass threads carrying messages from people I love.

Still, I have thought often about those quiet forty hours—about how vivid the room felt once the invisible cushion of convenience thinned out just enough for us to feel the weather again. The cold had weight. The tea tasted sharper. The conversation wandered for three hours without anyone checking a screen to settle a minor trivia dispute, leaving the small mystery hanging pleasantly in the air between us.

Perhaps the wisest posture toward the world is not to reject ease, nor to worship hardship for its own sake, but to choose our frictions deliberately. To notice where resistance is merely cruel waste, and where it is the very thing giving shape, flavor, and gravity to our days. To remember the diver splicing glass in the dark ocean, the painter scraping rust above the bay, the carpenter reading the curve of an oak board, and the simple physics of a shoe meeting the pavement.

We are not meant to hover an inch above our lives, gliding effortlessly from birth to death without leaving a scuff mark. We are meant to press down, feel the ground push back, and use that grip to walk somewhere worth going.
